How to read these panels

Generation by fuel type is the most recent five-minute reading. The strip is the mix as proportions; the rows beneath it are the same fuels as megawatts, ranked. A fuel can be negative — pumped storage consumes power while it refills, and an interconnector counts as negative when GB is exporting — so a fuel with no segment in the strip still has a row.

The 24-hour and 7-day views stack the same fuels over time. Height is total generation, so the shape of the top edge is the day’s demand curve seen from the supply side. The 7-day view is built from settled half-hourly data and lags the live reading by a few hours at the right-hand edge.

Wind against forecast shows outturn beside two vintages of the day-ahead forecast, and the error measure beneath is the mean absolute difference over the window. The improvement figure is the honest one to look at: it says how much closer the latest forecast got than the earliest, which is what forecasting is for.

⚠ Why no two sources agree on “GB generation”

This is the single most useful thing to understand about any electricity dashboard, including this one. There is no such quantity as the amount of electricity Great Britain is generating. There are several, they are all correct, and they differ by thousands of megawatts.

Metered generation is what the transmission system can see: large stations that settle through the Balancing Mechanism. It is the figure with the best provenance and it excludes a great deal of real electricity.

Embedded generation is everything connected to the local distribution networks instead — rooftop and field solar above all, plus smaller wind and gas. The transmission system never meters it; it sees only the demand that did not appear. So embedded output has to be estimated, and this page marks every estimated figure as such rather than quietly folding it into a total.

Interconnector flows are generation from the system’s point of view when they are importing and demand when they are exporting, which is why they change sign.

The mix on this page counts metered generation plus estimated embedded solar plus net imports, because that is what is actually available to consume in GB. A source quoting a smaller number has probably drawn the boundary at the transmission system; one quoting a larger number may be counting capacity rather than output. Neither is wrong. They are answers to different questions, and the boundary is the question.

Why “Other” cannot be broken down

Elexon publishes a category called OTHER and does not say what is in it. It is small, it is real, and it is genuinely unattributable from the published data — so this page shows it as its own row rather than distributing it across the fuels it might contain. Splitting it would make the table look more complete and every number in it less true.

What the carbon columns are doing

The last two columns of the detail table are the argument the fuel mix cannot make on its own. Share of generation and share of CO2 are the same fuels measured two ways, and they do not line up: gas is routinely under a third of the electricity and most of the carbon, while nuclear and wind are a large share of the electricity and almost none of the carbon.

The factors come from NESO’s published set, live where the feed answers. The interconnector row is a blend of the three published import factors and is labelled as one — the real carbon content of an import depends on what the neighbouring market happened to be running, which nobody publishes in real time.
